title: The pKa ladder
note: Lower pKa means stronger acid. Memorize the ladder from HCl (−7) down: carboxylic acids 4–5, phenol and ammonium about 10, water 15.7, alcohols 16–18, ketone α-H 19–20, alkyne 25, NH₃ 35–38, alkene C–H mid-40s, alkane 50 or higher. Equilibrium favors the weaker acid.

read.title: Climbing down the pKa ladder
text: Every proton transfer is a contest, and the pKa table tells you who wins. Acids sit on a ladder: HCl near −7, carboxylic acids at 4–5, phenols and alkylammonium ions around 10, water at 15.7, alcohols at 16–18, ketone α-hydrogens at 19–20, terminal alkynes at 25, ammonia at about 35–38, alkene C–H bonds in the mid-40s, and alkanes around 50 or higher. Textbooks differ by a unit or two on some entries, so trust the ordering more than any single digit.

The rule: an equilibrium favors the weaker acid, the one with the higher pKa. A base can deprotonate an acid only if the base's conjugate acid sits higher on the ladder. Hydroxide, whose conjugate acid is water at 15.7, takes a proton from acetic acid completely but barely touches an alkyne. Amide ion, NH₂⁻, with a conjugate acid near 35 to 38, does deprotonate an alkyne.

Why does the ladder look like this? Look at the conjugate base. Resonance spreads charge in carboxylates and phenoxides. Electronegativity favors O over N over C across a row. Size favors I over F down a column. Inductive withdrawal by nearby halogens stabilizes the anion. Hybridization matters too: sp carbon has more s character, which holds the lone pair closer to the nucleus.
